title: Stephen's Speech and the First Martyr
summary: Asked by the high priest whether the charges are true, Stephen retells Israel's history from Abraham to Solomon, showing that God met his people outside the land and that Israel repeatedly rejected the leaders God sent, from Joseph to Moses to the prophets. He argues that the Most High does not dwell in houses made by human hands and accuses the council of resisting the Holy Spirit and murdering the Righteous One. Enraged, they drag him out and stone him, while he sees Jesus standing at God's right hand and prays for his killers; a young man named Saul watches.
story: Stephen was charged in chapter 6 with speaking against the temple and the law. This chapter is his answer and his death. It is the longest speech in Acts and marks the end of the Jerusalem period of the church's witness (1:8). Stephen's death triggers the persecution that scatters believers into Judea and Samaria (8:1), and his vision and prayer are witnessed by Saul, who will soon become the church's greatest missionary. The chapter looks back over the whole story of Israel from Genesis to the monarchy and forward to the gospel's spread beyond the temple and the land.
historical:
Stephen's trial takes place before the Sanhedrin in Jerusalem, probably in the early to mid 30s AD. The question of how a Jewish council could carry out a stoning when John 18:31 says they were not permitted to execute is debated. Many scholars think the council's hearing turned into a mob action in the heat of anger, since Luke describes no formal sentence. Others suggest it happened during a gap in Roman oversight, and some date it to around AD 36 or 37, when Pilate had been recalled to Rome, though the date is uncertain. The law required execution by stoning outside the camp or city (Leviticus 24:14), with the witnesses throwing the first stones (Deuteronomy 17:7), which explains why they laid aside their outer garments.

Stephen's retelling of history follows the Greek translation of the Old Testament (the Septuagint), which many Diaspora Jews read, and sometimes blends traditions. His quotation from Amos 5:25-27 follows the Septuagint's reading Rephan, the name of a star deity, and says beyond Babylon where Amos had beyond Damascus, applying the prophecy to the later exile to Babylon. The number seventy-five for Jacob's family matches the Septuagint of Genesis 46:27 and Exodus 1:5 (the Hebrew text has seventy), and a Hebrew manuscript of Exodus from the Dead Sea Scrolls also reads seventy-five.
cultural:
The temple was the center of Jewish national and religious life, and to speak of it critically was dangerous. It was also a symbol of Israel's identity, heavily associated with the promise of God's presence. Stephen does not deny that God commanded the tabernacle or that Solomon built the temple; he argues that God's presence was never confined to it. Isaiah 66:1-2, which he quotes, already said this. His phrase made by human hands was a phrase Jews commonly used of idols, so applying it to a mindset about the temple was deeply provocative.

Stiff-necked and uncircumcised in heart and ears are the language of the Law and the Prophets themselves (Exodus 33:5; Deuteronomy 10:16; Jeremiah 6:10). Stephen is speaking as a Jewish prophet within Israel, using Israel's own Scriptures, not as an outsider attacking the Jewish people. Gnashing the teeth expressed fury. Covering the ears was a reaction to what the hearers took as blasphemy, which they would not listen to.
literary: The speech is arranged around three great figures, Abraham (2-8), Joseph (9-16), and Moses (17-43), followed by the tabernacle and temple (44-50) and a direct accusation (51-53). Two threads run through it. First, God meets his people outside the holy land: in Mesopotamia, in Egypt, in Midian, at Sinai, so God's presence is not confined to the temple. Second, Israel repeatedly rejected the deliverers God sent: the brothers sold Joseph; the Israelites pushed Moses away and turned to idols; the fathers killed the prophets. The speech builds toward the Righteous One whom the council betrayed and murdered. The narrative of Stephen's death echoes Jesus' death in Luke: he commits his spirit to the Lord and prays for his killers' forgiveness (Luke 23:34, 46). Luke closes with a gentle phrase for a violent death: he fell asleep.

outline.t: Abraham: called and promised outside the land
Joseph: rejected by his brothers, raised up by God
Moses: born, raised, and rejected as deliverer
Moses: sent at the bush and leading in the wilderness
Tabernacle and temple: God does not dwell in houses made by hands
You always resist the Holy Spirit

doctrines.note: Stephen retells Israel's history as God's story of promise and deliverance. He appeals to the law received through angels as living words, and he reads the prophets as pointing to the Righteous One. His argument assumes that Israel's Scriptures, read rightly, lead to Jesus.

Stephen names the golden calf, the worship of the host of heaven, and the works of their hands. He suggests that even a good gift, the temple, can become an object of trust in place of God himself. Idolatry is not only bowing to statues but confining God to what we have made.

Stephen is the first Christian martyr, and he dies seeing heaven open and praying for his killers. His death shows that faithful witness may cost everything, and that God's presence and glory are revealed even in the place of suffering.

Stephen asks the Lord Jesus to receive his spirit and then falls asleep, the New Testament's common way of describing the death of believers. The phrase does not deny the reality of death, but it expresses hope in the resurrection.

words.note: Doxa, glory: the visible splendor and weight of God's presence. Stephen begins his speech with the God of glory who appeared to Abraham in Mesopotamia, far from any temple, and ends his life seeing the glory of God and Jesus standing at God's right hand. The frame makes his point: God's glory is not confined to one building.

Paroikos, a foreigner or resident alien, someone living in a land not his own. Stephen uses it of Abraham's descendants in Egypt (7:6) and of Moses in Midian (7:29). Israel's great figures were often strangers. First Peter 2:11 uses the same word for Christians in the world, as sojourners whose true home is with God.

Apotheo, to push away or reject. It is used for the Israelite who pushed Moses aside (7:27) and for the fathers who rejected him in the wilderness (7:39). The word ties together the story's pattern: those God sends to deliver his people are thrust away, as Jesus was.

christ: The whole speech points toward Jesus without naming him until its end. Joseph, rejected by his brothers and then raised up to save them, and Moses, rejected by his people but sent by God as ruler and redeemer, are patterns of the Righteous One whom the leaders betrayed. Moses himself foretold a prophet like him (7:37). The true dwelling place of God is not a building but, as the rest of the New Testament will show, the risen Christ and his people. Stephen's vision of the Son of Man standing at God's right hand recalls Daniel 7:13-14 and Jesus' own words at his trial (Luke 22:69). Many readers take Jesus' standing as rising to welcome his servant, others as standing as a witness or advocate in the heavenly court, others as standing to judge. Stephen's dying prayers show how completely he had been formed by his Lord.

hard.q: Stephen's history seems to differ from Genesis in several details. Did he, or Luke, make mistakes?
hard.a:
Careful readers have long noticed several difficulties. Genesis 12 places God's call to Abraham in Haran, while Stephen places it in Mesopotamia before Haran. Stephen says the tomb at Shechem was bought by Abraham from the sons of Hamor, while Genesis says Abraham bought the cave of Machpelah at Hebron from Ephron (Genesis 23) and Jacob bought land at Shechem from Hamor's sons (Genesis 33:19). The number seventy-five follows the Greek rather than the Hebrew text.

Responses differ. Some point out that other passages already imply a call in Ur (Genesis 15:7; Nehemiah 9:7), that Jewish tradition sometimes telescoped events and burial places, and that Stephen summarizes the story of the patriarchs as a whole rather than listing each transaction. Others think Stephen, speaking under pressure, blended traditions in ways a careful scholar would not, and that Luke faithfully recorded what he said without correcting it. Still others simply regard these as errors in the account. None of these details affects Stephen's argument, which is about God's presence beyond the land and Israel's rejection of those God sent.

questions: Stephen's speech shows God meeting his people in foreign lands, deserts, and prisons. Where have you met God outside the places you expected?
Stephen accuses his hearers of always resisting the Holy Spirit. In what ways might religious people today resist God while thinking they are defending him?
Stephen prayed for those who were killing him. What would it take for you to pray that way for those who wrong you?
